prompt: Which table lock does a plain `SELECT` take on the table it reads?

choices.text: None: readers in PostgreSQL never lock anything
choices.why: Readers take no row locks, but window B saw AccessShareLock on orders and all four of its indexes.

choices.text: ACCESS SHARE
choices.why: Right: the weakest mode, which conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

choices.text: ROW SHARE, on each row it returns
choices.why: ROW SHARE is a table mode, taken by SELECT … FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE, not by a plain read.

choices.text: SHARE, which lets other readers in and keeps writers out
choices.why: That is what CREATE INDEX takes; a SELECT that blocked writers would make every report stop the shop.

prompt: Window A has an open transaction that updated one order. Which of these, typed in window B, waits for it?

choices.text: `UPDATE` of a different order
choices.why: Two ROW EXCLUSIVE locks do not conflict, and different rows do not either: it went through in under 3 ms.

choices.text: `SELECT count(*) FROM orders`
choices.why: ACCESS SHARE does not conflict with ROW EXCLUSIVE; readers go ahead.

choices.text: `CREATE INDEX` on `orders`
choices.why: Right: CREATE INDEX takes SHARE, which conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE; it waited 8985 ms in the lesson.

choices.text: `VACUUM orders`
choices.why: VACUUM takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which does not conflict with ROW EXCLUSIVE.

prompt: Why does a transaction that ran one `SELECT` an hour ago and is still open matter to a later `ALTER TABLE`?

choices.text: Its ACCESS SHARE lasts until the transaction ends
choices.why: Right: locks are collected and released together at COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so the ALTER waits for the whole transaction.

choices.text: It does not: the SELECT finished, so its lock was released when the rows came back
choices.why: Nothing is released early; the lock outlives the statement and lasts as long as the transaction.

choices.text: Its snapshot keeps the ALTER from seeing the table
choices.why: Snapshots decide which row versions are visible; the wait comes from the lock.

choices.text: It holds row locks on every row it read
choices.why: A plain SELECT locks no rows.

prompt: A nightly job runs `CREATE INDEX` on a 400-million-row table, and the shop's checkout times out until it finishes. What would have kept checkout working?
hint: Which mode does each form take?

choices.text: Running it inside a transaction so it can be rolled back
choices.why: A transaction changes nothing about the SHARE lock it holds while building.

choices.text: Setting `lock_timeout` on the job
choices.why: lock_timeout limits the wait to get the lock; once granted, the build still blocks writes for its whole length.

choices.text: Building it `CONCURRENTLY`
choices.why: Right: SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lets INSERT and UPDATE through, which plain CREATE INDEX's SHARE does not.

choices.text: Running ANALYZE first
choices.why: Statistics have nothing to do with the lock the build takes.

prompt: How many table lock modes does PostgreSQL have?
Window A has updated order 1 and not committed. What does a plain `SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = 1` in window B do?

choices.text: Waits until window A commits
choices.why: A plain read is never blocked by a row lock.

choices.text: Fails with `could not obtain lock`
choices.why: That error came from FOR UPDATE NOWAIT, not from a plain read.

choices.text: Shows window A's change, since it is already in the table
choices.why: Uncommitted changes are invisible to other transactions; it read delivered.

choices.text: Answers at once with the old value
choices.why: Right: it read `delivered`, the version from before window A's update.

prompt: Window B waited 7085 ms on `SELECT status … FOR UPDATE` and then read `shipped`, not `delivered`. Why that value?

choices.text: It reads the row once the lock is granted, after window A's commit
choices.why: Right: after window A committed, so it sees the committed change, which is what makes FOR UPDATE then UPDATE safe.

choices.text: Window B's transaction had started after window A committed
choices.why: Window B began its transaction before the commit; it was waiting when window A committed.

choices.text: FOR UPDATE always reads the newest uncommitted version
choices.why: No read sees another transaction's uncommitted change.

choices.text: The SELECT was run twice by psql
choices.why: psql sent it once; the server waited and then read.

prompt: Ten packing stations run `UPDATE … WHERE id IN (SELECT … LIMIT 3 FOR UPDATE)` at the same time. What happens without `SKIP LOCKED`?

choices.text: Two stations get the same three orders
choices.why: The lock prevents that; window B re-read and took the next three.

choices.text: One station works at a time, the rest in line
choices.why: Right: window B waited 7495 ms for window A's rows before taking the next three.

choices.text: Nine get a deadlock error
choices.why: They wait in the same direction, so no cycle forms.

choices.text: The statement fails because LIMIT is not allowed with FOR UPDATE
choices.why: It ran in the lesson and returned three ids.

prompt: A finance report uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` 'so that it never waits'. What is wrong with it?
hint: What does SKIP LOCKED leave out?

choices.text: SKIP LOCKED works only inside an UPDATE
choices.why: It works on any SELECT … FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE.

choices.text: It locks the whole table for the report's duration
choices.why: It locks the rows it returns and takes ROW SHARE on the table, which blocks almost nothing.

choices.text: Rows others have locked are silently left out of its totals
choices.why: Right: SKIP LOCKED is an inconsistent view on purpose, made for queues; a report built on it is wrong whenever writes are happening.

choices.text: It makes the report deadlock with every writer
choices.why: Skipping never waits, so it cannot be part of a wait cycle.

prompt: `SELECT … FOR UPDATE ___` raises an error at once instead of waiting when the row is locked.
hint: One word, the opposite of waiting.

prompt: In the three-window experiment, what was window C's `SELECT` actually waiting for?
hint: Its lock does not conflict with window A's.

choices.text: Window A's ACCESS SHARE
choices.why: Two ACCESS SHARE locks do not conflict; window A alone would not have stopped it.

choices.text: Window B's ALTER
choices.why: Right: a request is granted only if it conflicts with nobody holding the lock and nobody already queued.

choices.text: A row lock on order 2
choices.why: Nobody had touched order 2 in that experiment.

choices.text: The disk
choices.why: One row by primary key is a fraction of a millisecond; 12 seconds was a lock wait.

prompt: How many seconds did window C wait to read one order behind the waiting `ALTER TABLE`?
Why does the server not let a new reader jump past a waiting `ALTER TABLE` when the reader conflicts with nothing that is held?
hint: Think of a busy table with readers arriving all the time.

choices.text: Because readers are slower than writers
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with the queue rule.

choices.text: Because the reader would see the half-altered table
choices.why: The ALTER has not started; it is still waiting for its lock.

choices.text: Because ACCESS SHARE conflicts with every other mode
choices.why: It conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

choices.text: The ALTER would never get in: some reader would always hold the table
choices.why: Right: the queue is what stops a strong lock starving, and the price is that everyone behind it waits.

prompt: A migration adds a column to `orders` at 10:00 with `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` and fails with `canceling statement due to lock timeout`. What should the deploy do next?
hint: The timeout did its job; the change still has to happen.

choices.text: Raise lock_timeout to an hour so it cannot fail
choices.why: That brings back the outage: an hour in the queue with every query behind it.

choices.text: Try again shortly, in a loop, keeping the short timeout
choices.why: Right: each attempt costs the application at most two seconds, and one of them gets in once the long transaction ends.

choices.text: Use statement_timeout instead, which is stricter
choices.why: statement_timeout would also cut off the slow reports; it does not target the wait for a lock.

choices.text: Restart the server to clear every lock, then run the migration
choices.why: A restart is an outage for everybody to solve a two-second wait.

prompt: What does `pg_try_advisory_lock(42)` return when another session already holds lock 42?

choices.text: It waits until the other session releases it
choices.why: That is pg_advisory_lock without try, which window B then ran and waited 6434 ms.

choices.text: An error
choices.why: It returns a boolean; nothing is raised.

choices.text: `f`, at once
choices.why: Right: try never waits; it answers t or f.

choices.text: The process id of the session that holds it
choices.why: It returns only whether this session got the lock.

prompt: Why is an advisory lock better than a `status = 'running'` row for making sure a nightly job runs once?
hint: What happens when the worker crashes halfway?

choices.text: A crash releases the lock but not the row
choices.why: Right: nothing can be left behind, so the next night's run is never blocked by a dead worker.

choices.text: Advisory locks are faster to write
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; a row update takes a millisecond too.

choices.text: A status row cannot be read by other workers
choices.why: Any worker can read the row; the trouble is a row nobody clears after a crash.

choices.text: Advisory locks survive a server restart
choices.why: They do not survive; they belong to sessions, and a restart ends every session.

prompt: An application behind a transaction-mode pooler takes `pg_advisory_lock(7)` in one transaction and unlocks it in the next. Jobs start getting stuck. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: Advisory locks are disabled behind poolers
choices.why: The pooler does not disable them; it changes which connection holds them.

choices.text: The number 7 is reserved by PostgreSQL
choices.why: No numbers are reserved; the meaning is entirely the application's.

choices.text: The unlock ran on another connection
choices.why: Right: a session-level lock belongs to one connection, and the pooler gave the next transaction a different one; transaction-level locks avoid it.

choices.text: Two transactions cannot use one lock number
choices.why: They can, one after the other; that is the normal use.

prompt: Why did window B's statement fail after almost exactly 1001 ms?
hint: A setting with a one-second default.

choices.text: lock_timeout, which the lesson had set to one second
choices.why: That was set to two seconds, in another window, in section 04; the error here was deadlock detected.

choices.text: A waiting session only checks for a deadlock after `deadlock_timeout`
choices.why: Right: checking on every wait would be expensive, so the check runs once the wait reaches one second.

choices.text: The update took one second to find the row
choices.why: Finding one row by primary key takes a fraction of a millisecond.

choices.text: psql gives up on any statement after one second of silence from the server
choices.why: psql waits indefinitely; earlier waits in this lesson lasted over 13 seconds.

prompt: Both windows run `SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id IN (…) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` before updating orders 1 and 2. Why can no deadlock form?

choices.text: FOR UPDATE takes a table lock that serialises the two
choices.why: It takes ROW SHARE, which does not conflict with itself; the order of the row locks is what matters.

choices.text: deadlock_timeout is disabled for SELECT
choices.why: No such exception exists.

choices.text: The IN list is sorted by the server
choices.why: The list order does not matter; the ORDER BY decides the order the rows are locked in.

choices.text: Both take order 1 first
choices.why: Right: window B waited on order 1 before locking anything, so no cycle could close.

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's deadlock in the order they happened.
hint: Each window takes one order first.
items: Window A asks for order 2 and waits
Window B asks for order 1 and waits
After one second, window B's check finds the cycle and its statement fails
trap: Window A's update of order 2 finishes only after window B's transaction has failed and released it.

prompt: Match each error or symptom to what causes it.

pairs.right: FOR UPDATE NOWAIT on a row somebody holds
a lock not granted within lock_timeout
two transactions waiting for each other
a request queued behind a waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE

right_distractors: a missing index on the column

prompt: Which of these are habits the lesson recommends for a schema change on a busy table? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Set lock_timeout to a few seconds first
choices.why: Right: it takes the ALTER out of the queue before the queue hurts.

choices.text: Retry in a loop when it times out
choices.why: Right: each attempt costs a short hiccup, and one gets in.

choices.text: Look for long transactions before starting
choices.why: Right: they are what the ALTER would queue behind.

choices.text: Run it inside a long transaction with the data fix, so both happen together
choices.why: A long transaction holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for its whole length, the opposite of what you want.

choices.text: Raise deadlock_timeout so the ALTER is not cancelled
choices.why: deadlock_timeout decides when cycles are checked; it does nothing for a queue.
